extracted.intended_audience: scholars, policy analysts, and regulators studying administrative rulemaking, lobbying, and notice-and-comment processes
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and theoretical criteria for assessing how interest groups (via meetings and public comments) affect agency rulemaking outcomes and how to measure those effects using high-frequency event studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of agency discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of real policymaking slack an agency has — increases with hard-to-write legislation, short-sighted Congress, costly/ conflicted court enforcement, hard-to-observe agency actions/information, and complexity of the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher agency discretion creates more opportunity for distributive politics and makes interest-group engagement more likely to change outcomes. Use assessments of statutory ambiguity, oversight capacity, and enforcement cost to judge discretion. Anti-pattern: assuming delegation equals no discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of participation relative to rule development
rubrics_metrics.description: When stakeholders engage the agency (pre-proposal rule-development meetings, meetings during notice-and-comment, or comment letters at proposal/finalization) matters for influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings before a proposal (rule development) are expected to be the most effective because agency staff have the most discretion then. Comments come later when discretion is smaller and harder to influence senior decision-makers. Empirical strategy should separate proposal and finalization announcements. Avoid pooling all engagements without respect to timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting officials with available discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence depends on whether engagement reaches the organizational level that actually has decision-making discretion at that moment (often 'mezzo-level' rule-team staff rather than agency heads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize meetings or communications that reach staff who set the policy space early. Evaluate records (meeting logs, attendance) to see if participants met the staff with decision authority. Anti-pattern: assuming contact with agency leaders is the only relevant access point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel accessibility versus efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments are widely accessible (available to all) but often less effective at producing particularistic benefits; meetings are less accessible (selective) but more likely to produce particularistic policy changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising stakeholders or evaluating influence, weigh the tradeoff: comments offer democratic access but face barriers to reaching key decision-makers; meetings can be more persuasive but create equity/transparency concerns. For research, treat channels separately rather than aggregating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of persuasive 'goods' interest groups provide
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest groups can provide information (credible, verifiable), political support (commitments to fight), signals of public preference, or reputation-building; agencies value these heterogeneous goods differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting comments or meetings, tailor the communication to the 'good' valued by the agency (technical evidence, implementation data, political-mobilization signals). For evaluation, categorize submissions by type (information vs political signal) to test which correlate with outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity versus vagueness of requested policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders may ask for specific, concrete rule changes (definitions, formula tweaks, exemptions) or for vaguer/flexible standards that leave room for agency discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific requests can make compliance/implementation clearer and easier to evaluate; vagueness can preserve future negotiation/flexibility. Consider strategic motives: incumbents may request exclusion (specificity) while others ask for vagueness to enable later bargaining. For content analysis, code requests along this axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of common requests in comments/meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical asks include: treating the sender like competitors (parity), treating the sender differently (exemption or carve-out), asking for delays in implementation, requesting withdrawal of the rule, asking to extend comment windows, and formula/weighting changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing comment letters/meetings, categorize the request type. Examples from Dodd–Frank include price-cap adjustments, exclusions from definitions, implementation delays, or requests to withdraw. Use this taxonomy to link requests to observed policy concessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing comment content to rule texts to detect concessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether comment requests map onto changes in the proposed/final rule by directly comparing comment demands to language and provisions in rule texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A content-analysis approach can reveal pervasive policy concessions that correlate with market outcomes. Use systematic coding (e.g., whether rule language mirrors comment phrasing) and document examples. Be wary of over-attribution without temporal and causal checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-study outcome: standardized returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure firm-level market reaction to rule announcements using standardized returns Y_dt_it = (P_dt_it − P_0_it) / (P_0_it * sqrt(dt) * σ_i), where σ_i is minute-to-minute volatility and dt is minutes after event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization addresses heteroskedasticity/volatility differences across firms. Use this or equivalent standardization to make returns comparable across firms and time horizons. Report formula and volatility estimation details. Anti-pattern: using raw price changes without volatility adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of time horizon (dt) for measuring market reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of dt (e.g., 1 minute, 20 minutes, 1 hour, 3 hours) affects estimated returns: shorter dt reduces confounding but may miss information processing; longer dt risks contemporaneous confounders but captures market frictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be principled: prefer smaller dt to limit confounding but balance against market processing speed. The paper uses one hour as a compromise. Present sensitivity across multiple dt values as robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of treatment indicators (τ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalize lobbying actions as indicators (e.g., τ^−_it = met before proposal, τ^+_it = met during notice-and-comment, τ^C_it = commented) treated as dichotomous or counts; consider vector-valued τ to capture multiple actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly define treatment timing and whether multiple treatments can co-occur. In robustness checks, consider count specifications. Avoid conflating different action types into a single undifferentiated treatment variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of counterfactual/comparison group
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible benchmarks include: (a) no-return baseline (random times), (b) all passive competitors, or (c) the most similar competitors matched on covariates; each has tradeoffs re: free-riding and selection bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple comparison groups and explain limitations. Most-similar matches reduce selection bias but may understate effects if passive firms free-ride; all competitors are less prone to free-riding bias but more subject to selection differences. Present results across benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching on propensity to lobby
rubrics_metrics.description: Create matched controls using covariates that predict lobbying: economic resources, legal sophistication, prior investment in political influence; analyst coverage predicts lower participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate propensity scores and match treated firms to the most similar untreated firms. Report balance diagnostics. Include sensitivity checks. Avoid using poorly predictive covariates that leave residual confounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression controls and fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Include controls or fixed effects (e.g., rule fixed effects, firm fixed effects, covariates used for matching) to account for heterogeneity in regulations and firm characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rule fixed effects to control for regulation-specific shocks and firm fixed effects where appropriate. Explain that some firms or rules may cause inordinately strong movements and control accordingly. Report specification checks with and without those controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and falsification tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct placebo tests, falsification exercises, permutation tests, and alternative specifications (e.g., count treatments, different dt) to bolster inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a battery of robustness checks to show results are not artefacts. The paper emphasizes multiple placebo and falsification tests in the Appendix. Anti-pattern: relying on a single specification without robustness evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for spillovers and SUTVA violations (free-riding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that lobbying by one firm can affect competitors (spillovers), violating no-interference assumptions and biasing estimates (typically toward underestimation if passive firms free-ride).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss and where possible model spillovers; interpret estimates as lower bounds if free-riding is likely. Consider alternative designs or comparison groups less able to free-ride, but note tradeoffs with selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of event timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify announcement time precisely (e.g., using Board press releases, RSS timestamps, server publication times obtained via FOIA) to measure minute-by-minute market reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-precision timestamps reduce measurement error in event windows. Document time-source and handling of ambiguous timestamps. Avoid coarse or imprecise timing that can smear effects across windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling heteroskedasticity in returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Because returns exhibit heterogeneous volatility across firms, standardize returns by firm-specific minute-to-minute volatility to make cross-firm comparisons valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate σ_i robustly and use it in the standardized-return formula. Report how volatility was computed and sensitivity to different volatility windows. Do not ignore heteroskedasticity in event-study returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separating proposal and final-rule analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat proposed-rule announcements (tp) and final-rule announcements (tf) as distinct events with separate panels and analyses, since they may have different informational content and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run separate event studies for proposals and final rules. Be explicit about which announcements are being analyzed in each figure/table. Avoid collapsing proposal and final announcement effects into a single event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting causality with observational data
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about causal claims: observational event studies require assumptions about counterfactuals (e.g., outcomes would be like passive competitors or baseline expectations). Selection into lobbying complicates inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame causal statements conditionally, discuss plausible counterfactuals, and present matching/controls and falsification tests. Explicitly enumerate assumptions and alternative explanations (market efficiency, firm ability to respond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize graphical presentation complemented by formal estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear graphical illustrations of average returns by treatment status to show patterns, and reserve formal regressions (with matching, controls) for robustness and estimation in appendices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphs aid intuition; formal models provide tests. Report both and explain the role of each. Avoid relying solely on regression tables without visualizing event dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational and temporal distribution of discretion within agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency rulemaking authority is sub-delegated to teams and departments; discretion is larger earlier and concentrated in rule-team staff, and staff investments create path dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze who attended meetings (e.g., staff vs agency heads) and when decisions were effectively made. Consider staff data-collection/investments (surveys, studies) that lock in policy paths. Anti-pattern: assuming agency heads always control key discretionary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff investments and sunk-cost stickiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff investments (surveys, data collection, policy design work) before proposal increase the cost of reversing early discretionary choices and make those early choices sticky in the proposed/final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing scope for influence, document staff investments and show how early investments constrain later changes. Use examples (e.g., issuer-cost survey that produced price-cap figures) to illustrate stickiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish particularistic versus universal benefits sought
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whether requested changes are narrow/firm-specific (particularistic) or broadly applicable (universal), as this affects the incentives for other firms to free-ride and the likely channels for influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code comments/meeting materials for whether asks are particularistic (e.g., carve-outs, definition changes) or universal (e.g., delay for all). Particularistic asks are more likely pursued via meetings; universal asks may be more common in comments but distributional impact still varies across firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing and validating similarity matches
rubrics_metrics.description: When using matched comparisons, construct matches on observable covariates that predict lobbying and validate similarity (market capitalization, legal sophistication, prior political investment, industry exposure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report balance tests and show descriptive comparisons between treated firms and their matched controls. Use closest competitors as one matching approach. Acknowledge untestable assumptions about unobserved confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy transparency recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given evidence meetings are associated with larger distributive gains and meetings are less transparent, policymakers should consider increasing transparency about agency-stakeholder meetings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: enhance meeting logs, publication of meeting materials, and broader access to rule-development interactions to reduce inequities. Use empirical findings on disproportionate meeting access (e.g., large banks) to motivate reforms.
